REACHABILITY.reasoning: The window is real. AtomicFileWrite.swift:19 writes the temp file with the default mode, and the chmod to 0600 only comes at :20-24. But the only secret-bearing write another local user could reach is the Codex write-back (FileCredentialReader.swift:74), and that path is not reachable in the default deploy. OpenAIProvider.swift:76 and :92 call refresh/writeBack only when manageOAuthRefresh is true. That flag defaults to false in AppConfig.swift:309/326/350/364 and in the provider init parameters (OpenAIProvider.swift:38/49), and CLAUDE.md treats read-only as a hard rule. The other 0o600 callers (ConfigLoader.swift:110/189/276, DiskCache.swift:135, UsageHistoryStore.swift:152, OpenAIResetJournal.swift:30) write into the app's Application Support and Caches dirs, which the app forces to 0700, so another user cannot get to their temp files; the finding admits this itself. The claimed attack also stacks unproven conditions: a multi-user Mac, a ~/.codex that others can traverse (nothing in the repo sets this dir's mode, so its permissions are not shown), and winning a race window of microseconds. The attacker's source is not reachable in the standard configuration, so the attack path is incomplete.

IMPACT.reasoning: If an attacker reaches this path, the claimed damage is real. The write only happens after opt-in (manage_oauth_refresh=true, OpenAIProvider.swift:38 defaults to false), and the severity stays LOW. AtomicFileWrite.swift:19 uses Data.write(.atomic), which gives the new tmp file the default mode (0666 & ~umask, so 0644) and fills it with the full JSON payload. The chmod to 0600 only runs afterwards at :20-24. Nothing narrows the mode before the plaintext lands. FileCredentialReader.swift:58-74 writes access_token, refresh_token and id_token into that tmp file in ~/.codex. On this machine the home dir is drwxr-x--- justoeu:staff, which every standard local user can traverse through the staff group, and ~/.codex is 0755. So during that window another local user can open() the .auth.json.<uuid>.tmp file. The fd keeps its read access after the chmod and the rename. What leaks is the rotated Codex refresh_token, a long-lived credential that allows session takeover, so the data is sensitive. The doc comment at :8-12 claims the race is avoided but it only moved from the final path to the tmp path, and a comment is not a mitigation. Limits: the window is short and there are two preconditions, a multi-user Mac and the non-default opt-in. config.toml writes land in the 0700 app-support dir and are not exposed.

DEFENSES.reasoning: The code pattern is real. AtomicFileWrite.swift:19 writes the full payload with Data.write(.atomic), and the 0o600 chmod only runs afterwards at :20-24, so the doc comment at :8-12 overstates what it does. The attack as written still does not hold up. (1) It only works through the Codex write-back at FileCredentialReader.swift:74, which runs only when manage_oauth_refresh is true. That setting is off by default for both the struct and the decoder (AppConfig.swift:309/326 and 350/364). The finding lists this as a precondition, so the claim depends on a non-default configuration. (2) Every other 0o600 caller writes into the app's own Application Support or Caches directories. The finding itself says those are forced to 0700, so another local user cannot even see the temp file there. That covers ConfigLoader.swift:110/189/276, DiskCache.swift:135/152, UsageHistoryStore.swift:152 and OpenAIResetJournal.swift:30. (3) The window only opens if Foundation's atomic write leaves the file at 0666&~umask rather than 0600. That code is closed-source Foundation and I could not confirm it by reading anything in this repo. It also needs a second local OS user who can traverse ~/.codex. What remains is a hardening gap: an opt-in setting on a multi-user Mac, plus unverified framework behaviour. That does not meet the standard of a complete attack path with no mitigation in the default deployment. The fix is still worth doing: use open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW, 0o600) and fchmod before writing.

REACHABILITY.reasoning: The code path the finding describes does exist and runs in the default deploy. KeychainCredentialReader.swift:36 sets fallback to SecurityToolCredentialReader() by default. IMPACT.reasoning: The code matches the description. DEFENSES.reasoning: The code gap is real. REACHABILITY.reasoning: The code does what the finding says. With the default config, no pinning runs. pin_hosts defaults to [] (AppConfig.swift:106/119). AppEnvironment.swift:30 then builds a plain HTTPClient(), and HTTPClient.swift:39-40 returns an unpinned client for an empty list. So the baseline entries in PinBaseline.swift:44-57 are never used by default, and the UI strings in en.lproj/Localizable.strings:153/190/210 are wrong when they say the baseline pins are active. The attack still does not hold up under this lens. There is no attacker-controlled source in the default deployment: the attack needs a forged certificate that the victim's system already trusts. The listed ways to get one are a corporate TLS-inspection proxy, an MDM profile, malware that installed a root CA, or a CA mis-issuance. A proxy or MDM profile is installed by whoever manages the machine. A malware root CA requires admin-level trust changes, and an attacker with that access can read the credential stores directly. Mis-issuance is speculative, and no code path shows it. Also, the same OAuth tokens are read from the Keychain item and ~/.codex/auth.json that the Claude Code and Codex CLIs keep current, and those CLIs call the same hosts using only system trust. An attacker who controls a trusted CA gets the tokens from them anyway, so this app is not what gives the attacker access. What is left is a missing extra layer of protection plus misleading UI text and doc comments, which is a documentation and correctness bug. The standard of proof requires a demonstrated attacker-controlled source, so the vote is FALSE_POSITIVE.

IMPACT.reasoning:

DEFENSES.reasoning: Nothing between the source and the sink stops this. 1) Source: under the default config, a certificate issued by any root the system trusts is accepted for vendor hosts. pinHosts defaults to [] (AppConfig.swift:106 and :119). 2) Dangerous operation: AppEnvironment.swift:30-37 installs HTTPClient() with the shared ephemeral session and no delegate when pinHosts is empty. REACHABILITY.reasoning: The mmap sink is real: ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:91 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 do use Data(contentsOf:options:[.mappedIfSafe]). Those directories belong to the user and are not a boundary another principal can cross. For benign cases, the scanner's own comment and memo logic treat transcripts as append-only (ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:75-77). No normal writer (Claude Code CLI or Codex CLI) shrinks a file mid-scan, so nobody reaches the truncation path in the default deploy. The source is not attacker-controlled across any boundary, so point 1 of the proof standard fails. At most this is a robustness bug in how the app reads files, not an exploitable vulnerability.

IMPACT.reasoning: The mmap is real. ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:91 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 map the files with Data(contentsOf:options:[.mappedIfSafe]), so a file that shrinks mid-scan can in theory raise SIGBUS. The claimed damage does not hold up, though. The only source is write access to ~/.claude/projects or ~/.codex/sessions, which means code already running as the same user in the same single-user desktop session. That code can already kill the process directly (kill -9), delete or corrupt the config, read the same credentials, or stop the app from launching. Crashing the menu-bar app through a truncation race gives it nothing it did not already have: no privilege or trust boundary is crossed, and the finding itself says nothing is disclosed. It also cannot hurt integrity. A short read or crash cannot write to disk or change credentials, and the memo or cache just gets rebuilt on the next launch. A legitimate writer (the Claude or Codex CLI) only appends to these transcripts, and appending does not cause SIGBUS. Only shrinking a file does, so accidental real-world triggering is unlikely. The result is a robustness or hardening issue (a plain read would remove the SIGBUS window), not a security impact. The same pattern appears at UsageHistoryStore.swift:95 and 142 on app-owned files, with the same conclusion.

DEFENSES.reasoning: The code claim is accurate. ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:91 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 read files with Data(contentsOf:options:[.mappedIfSafe]). The only guards before the read are a size/mtime memo lookup (ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:77-88) and a Task.isCancelled check (:65). Neither stops a file from being truncated after it is mapped. The finding's own precondition is write access to ~/.claude/projects or ~/.codex/sessions. Those directories are owned by the same macOS user who runs the menu-bar app. The operating system's per-user isolation is the defense, and it holds: another user, a sandboxed process or a remote party cannot write there. A same-user process that can write there already has a strictly stronger way to cause the claimed harm. It can send kill -9 to the app, delete or edit its config, or change the credential files the app reads. The only claimed impact is a crash that repeats (denial of service). This path gives the attacker nothing they did not already have, so there is no mitigation missing across a boundary. Switching to a plain read would be a sensible robustness fix against a CLI truncating its own files, but that is a reliability issue, not a security finding.

REACHABILITY.reasoning: The overflow is real in the code, and the scan runs by default. OpencodeScanner.swift:141-142 sums $.tokens.output and $.tokens.reasoning, :186-187 read them as Int64, and :197 adds them with a bare checked `+` that clamps each value only from below. The finding says so itself: its precondition is 'another tool or a prompt-injected agent running as the same user'. On this local single-user desktop app, a process that can write that file already has the same power over this app. It can kill the process, edit ~/Library/Application Support/ai-taskbar/config.toml, or delete the caches. Crashing the menu-bar app through a malformed row crosses no trust boundary and gives the attacker nothing new. No remote or lower-privileged actor controls this input: opencode itself writes token counts from real usage, and the file is opened read-only (SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY, :108). A multi-row sum that overflows makes SQLite fail the step with an integer overflow error, so :211 returns nil. That leaves only the crafted single-row case, which again needs a same-user writer. Separately, as a robustness bug (not a security vulnerability), :197 should use CostAggregator.saturatingAdd to match the other scanners.

IMPACT.reasoning: The arithmetic is real. OpencodeScanner.swift:141-142 sums $.tokens.output and $.tokens.reasoning in SQLite. Lines 186-187 read them with sqlite3_column_int64, which saturates a REAL to Int64.max. Line 197 adds `max(0, output) + max(0, reasoning)` with Swift's checked `+`, and neither Package.swift nor the Makefile sets -Ounchecked, so Int64.max + 1 would trap. What does not hold up is the claimed security impact. The only precondition is write access to ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db as the same UID. That access already allows everything the 'persistent DoS' does and more: kill or delete the app, edit config.toml, remove its Application Support directory, or change opencode's token data to fake the cost numbers. No privilege, sandbox or trust boundary is crossed. The damage is limited to a local usage monitor, and the user can undo it by deleting the offending row. No confidentiality or integrity loss comes from the trap. Setting the precondition aside, this is a robustness bug: line 197 should use CostAggregator.saturatingAdd like the other scanners. It should be tracked as a correctness fix, not a security vulnerability.

DEFENSES.reasoning: Nothing in the code stops the trap. 1) Source: the SQL at OpencodeScanner.swift:136-151 reads sum($.tokens.output) and sum($.tokens.reasoning) from the JSON `data` column of opencode.db. OpencodeScanner.swift:186-187 turns them into Int with sqlite3_column_int64. That call clamps REALs to the Int64 range, and SQLite's sum() does not overflow on a single row, so a value of Int64.max gets through. 2) Operation: OpencodeScanner.swift:197 `max(0, output) + max(0, reasoning)` uses Swift's checked `+`, which traps on overflow. max(0, x) only sets a lower bound. There is no upper clamp, no &+, and no CostAggregator.saturatingAdd before this line. The saturating add inside CostAggregator.add (line 201) runs after the trap point, so it cannot help. 3) Nothing sits between the source and the operation: no sanity ceiling, no SQL-side min(), and a trap cannot be caught with do/try. Caveat on the threat model: the attacker must be able to write to opencode.db as the same user, or a malicious provider must return huge token counts that opencode then stores. So the impact is a local, persistent crash of the monitor app, and LOW severity is appropriate. Seen through the DEFENSES lens, though, no framework, type-system or code-level guard prevents the crash.
